quote: Wenn man analoge Fragen $f = l\varphi + m\psi$ behandeln, wo $l, \varphi$ $\psi, m$ quadratische Formen sind etc.
english: If one treats analogous questions f = lφ + mψ, where l, φ, ψ, m are quadratic forms, etc.
topic: Short notes listing problems: the curve described by a struck billiard ball with spin and friction, the 27 lines on a cubic surface treated via an equation f = lφ + mψ and coincidence of solutions, analogous questions for quadratic forms, reducing the determination of the group of an equation to a finiteness problem, and ternary or quaternary forms satisfying a quadratic identity.

triage.modern_statement: This is my best reading of a short note, not something the page states outright. On the cubic-surface side, writing a cubic form as f = lφ + mψ (l, m linear; φ, ψ quadratic) means the surface f = 0 contains the line l = m = 0. Counting these decompositions recovers the 27 lines. Hilbert's 'analogous question' with l, m, φ, ψ all quadratic forms would then be: when can a quaternary quartic form f be written as lφ + mψ with quadrics l, m, φ, ψ? Geometrically, that means the quartic surface f = 0 in P^3 contains the elliptic quartic curve l = m = 0, which is a complete intersection of two quadrics. The follow-up questions are how many such representations or curves there are, and which quartics have them. The word 'etc.' suggests Hilbert also meant higher-degree versions.
triage.answered_by: The case Hilbert would have hoped for, a finite count like the 27 lines, does not exist. Noether stated and Lefschetz proved (around 1921; the year is from memory, not from the sources) that a very general quartic surface, and more generally any very general surface of degree at least 4 in P^3, contains only curves that are complete intersections with other surfaces. So such a quartic has no decomposition f = lφ + mψ into quadrics. The quartics that do have one form a Noether–Lefschetz divisor. That divisor has been studied and enumerated in modern work, for example by Cukierman, Lopez and Vainsencher in 'Enumeration of surfaces containing an elliptic quartic curve' (arXiv 1209.3335), and in the paper on Hilbert's sums-of-squares cones by Blekherman, Hauenstein, Ottem, Ranestad and Sturmfels (arXiv 1107.1846; I recalled the authors and topic myself, the search snippet only showed the arXiv number).

evidence.claim: The Noether-Lefschetz theorem: all curves on a very general surface of degree at least 4 in P^3 are complete intersections (Picard number 1). So a very general quartic has no quartic elliptic curve, meaning no f = lφ + mψ with quadrics.
Noether and Lefschetz proved that a very general quartic surface has Picard number one.

Cukierman, Lopez and Vainsencher enumerate the surfaces of degree at least 4 in P^3 that contain an elliptic quartic curve, i.e. the Noether-Lefschetz locus matching Hilbert's decomposition with quadrics.
A study of Hilbert's cone Σ_{4,4} deals with quartic surfaces containing a degree-4 elliptic curve, using the Noether-Lefschetz theorem as its starting point.

triage.why: The note is very short, and reading it as 'quartic surfaces containing a complete intersection of two quadrics' is my own interpretation by analogy with the 27-lines setup. Under that reading the question was settled in the negative for general surfaces by the Noether–Lefschetz theorem. The special surfaces that do admit such decompositions (Noether–Lefschetz loci of K3 surfaces) are still being studied and enumerated. This note is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. If Hilbert meant something else, for example ternary forms or counting decompositions in another setting, this identification would not hold.
